reason: The obvious attack here is translation drift, and it fails. This line circulates in two English renderings and the wrong one would have been easy to ship: Martin McLaughlin's 1999 Cape translation gives definition 6 as a book which has never exhausted all it has to say to its readers, which is not this wording at all. So the NYRB article itself was opened rather than a quotation site, and it prints, under Patrick Creagh's credit, exactly: A classic is a book that has never finished saying what it has to say. That is the shipped wording to the letter, including the that rather than which that the aggregator sites vary on. Locator: also confirmed at the page. Definition 4 is Every rereading of a classic is as much a voyage of discovery as the first reading, definition 5 is Every reading of a classic is in fact a rereading, and definition 7 is the one about books bearing the traces of readings previous to ours. Our line sits sixth, between 5 and 7, exactly as the source says, and the piece runs to fourteen definitions. Attribution and scope: Calvino's own essay, first given as Perche leggere i classici in 1981 and published in this translation on 9 October 1986, so well before 1999; no scripture, film, lyric, proverb, business or oratory; nothing needing a warning. Tag: Essay, which is the form of the work. Source line: 121 characters, leads with the name, no dash, names the translator and the date of the translation whose wording it uses, as rule 4 requires of a translated line. Cap: shipped.js gives italo calvino at 1 of 3, from month 1, not banned, nothing shipped and no near opening, and the month's verdicts hold no second Calvino, so the one-per-month rule is safe. Theme: a book that has never finished speaking is the month's what stays, and it is a cheerful thing at six in the morning.
